purpose.visibility_claim: This formative assessment makes visible the learner's ability to evaluate their initial explanation, prioritise meaningful improvements, implement those improvements independently, and justify significant changes. The revised explanation is the principal evidence of developing capability. A single determinate interpretation check provides limited diagnostic evidence but does not establish the quality of the learner's writing.
purpose.stop_rationale: The assessment provides a deliberate transition from interpreting research evidence and comparing explanations to exercising evaluative judgement over the learner's own work. Learning Element 6 allocates approximately eight minutes to reconsideration and prioritisation. Learning Element 7 allocates approximately twelve minutes to independent revision and a brief rationale. The distinction makes it possible to examine both the learner's decisions about quality and their ability to implement those decisions.
purpose.forward_intent: The learner retains their initial explanation, revised explanation and reasons for significant changes for reflection in 'The feedback that changed the work'. The assessment provides formative evidence without assigning grades, imposing progression conditions or determining a subsequent pathway.
purpose.count_basis: The author did not prescribe a determinate component count. One single-answer multiple-choice item was selected in the evidence-purpose stage to provide a focused diagnostic check on the distinction between association and causation. Three additional non-determinate constructed performances are required by the commission: prioritised reconsideration, an independently revised explanation and a brief rationale. No additional determinate items are introduced.
purpose.evidence_rationale: The four elicitations provide complementary evidence across the three authoritative learning outcomes. The initial self-review reveals evaluative judgement and prioritisation. The single determinate item checks a consequential interpretive distinction. The independently revised explanation provides the principal evidence of applied capability. The brief rationale makes significant feedback-informed decisions visible. The arrangement avoids duplicative testing and protects independent writing time.

research_evidence_boundary.study_title: Study breaks and concentration among undergraduate students
research_evidence_boundary.status: Fictional illustrative research study with synthetic findings.
research_evidence_boundary.method: Observational survey of 200 undergraduate students using self-reported study habits and concentration.
research_evidence_boundary.supported_interpretation: In this illustrative survey, students who reported taking regular short study breaks were more likely to report good concentration than students who did not report taking regular short breaks.
interpretive_constraints: The study was observational rather than randomised.
Study habits and concentration were self-reported.
Students were not randomly assigned to groups.
Sleep, motivation, workload and study environment were not controlled.
Objectively measured concentration and academic performance were not established.
The sample cannot automatically be assumed to represent all undergraduate students.
No statistical significance, confidence interval or causal effect has been established.
The findings do not establish the optimal frequency or duration of study breaks.

formative_boundaries: The assessment does not award grades, certification or pass/fail status.
No automatic correctness judgement or runtime AI evaluation is applied to unrestricted writing.
The determinate item is checked only against its explicitly defined answer key.
No response determines access to subsequent learning activities.
The revised explanation must be independently constructed rather than reproduced from a model answer.
Learners select and justify their own substantive improvements.
Revision must not be reduced to proofreading.
All substantive research evidence is available within the assessment.
The study must remain explicitly identified as fictional and illustrative.
Both versions of the explanation and the reasons for significant changes are retained for subsequent reflection.

bring_forward.what: If you completed 'Your first explanation', revisit the explanation you wrote there. Also revisit your own comparisons, judgements and feedback-informed insights from 'Comparing explanations and judging quality'.
bring_forward.how_used: Use your original explanation as the starting point for identifying strengths and weaknesses. Draw on your comparative insights to decide which improvements matter most, then use those decisions to produce a revised explanation for the same non-specialist audience.

entry_assumptions: The learner has previously been invited to produce an independent initial explanation of the illustrative survey.
The learner has had opportunities to develop evidence-grounded interpretation through 'Understanding what the evidence warrants' and 'Checking the interpretation'.
The learner has had opportunities to compare contrasting explanations and develop evaluative judgements through 'Comparing explanations and judging quality'.
No particular earlier learner response or level of achievement is assumed.
The complete canonical research evidence is available within this assessment.
The intended audience for the explanation is non-specialist.
The complete formative assessment lasts approximately 20 minutes.
The initial and revised explanations and reasons for significant changes are needed for 'The feedback that changed the work'.

elicitations.evidence_ask: Elicit a criteria-informed self-review of the learner's initial explanation that identifies and prioritises two or three substantive improvements and provides reasons grounded in the research evidence and developing evaluative judgement.
elicitations.stimulus: Study breaks and concentration among undergraduate students is a fictional, illustrative study created for educational purposes. In an observational survey, 200 undergraduate students reported their study habits and concentration. Among 100 students who reported taking regular short breaks during independent study, 72 reported good concentration (72%). Among 100 students who did not report taking regular short breaks, 58 reported good concentration (58%). The difference was 14 percentage points. Students were not randomly assigned to take or avoid breaks. Study habits and concentration were self-reported, and potentially relevant factors such as sleep, motivation, workload and study environment were not controlled. The survey did not establish objectively measured concentration, academic performance, a causal effect or the best frequency or duration of breaks. The sample cannot automatically be assumed to represent all undergraduate students. No statistical significance or confidence interval has been established.

prompt.title: Learning Element 6: Reconsider your explanation
prompt.context: You are revisiting your own explanation of the fictional study for a non-specialist audience. Your task is to decide which changes would make the greatest difference to its quality.
prompt.task: Read your initial explanation alongside the study evidence. Identify two or three substantive improvements you would prioritise. For each, explain what you want to improve and why that change matters. Draw on the quality judgements you have developed through comparing explanations. You might consider numerical precision, use of evidence, causal language, uncertainty, relevant context or accessibility, but choose the changes that are most important for your own explanation.
prompt.response_expectation: Record two or three prioritised improvements, each with a brief justification. Focus on the quality of the explanation rather than minor proofreading changes.
prompt.suggested_length: Two or three short entries, each explaining an intended improvement and its reason.

response_workspace.intention: Prioritised learner-authored self-review consisting of two or three substantive improvement decisions and brief justifications.
response_workspace.guidance: Use your own explanation as the basis for these decisions. You do not need to address every possible quality consideration.

materials.body: Review your priorities against your original explanation. Have you identified changes that would improve what a non-specialist reader learns from it, rather than mainly correcting its surface wording? Consider whether each priority responds to a real weakness or opportunity in your own work, is supported by the study evidence, and has a clear reason. You do not need to address every quality consideration. A useful priority is one you can explain and act upon.

formative_return.forward_orientation: Use your prioritised changes as decisions to implement when you write your revised explanation. Keep the emphasis on improving the explanation itself, not simply listing what could be better.

elicitations.evidence_ask: Elicit one determinate judgement about the strongest conclusion warranted by the observational survey, distinguishing a reported association from unsupported claims of causation, objective performance or generalisability.
elicitations.stimulus: In the fictional illustrative observational survey, 72 of 100 students who reported taking regular short study breaks also reported good concentration. Among 100 students who did not report taking regular short breaks, 58 reported good concentration. The observed difference was 14 percentage points. The students were not randomly assigned, the measures were self-reported, and factors including sleep, motivation, workload and study environment were not controlled.

prompt.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the findings and method of this illustrative survey?

options.text: Taking regular short breaks caused a 14-percentage-point improvement in students' concentration.
Students who reported regular short breaks were more likely to report good concentration than those who did not, but the survey does not establish that breaks caused the difference.
Introducing regular short breaks will increase good concentration by 14% among undergraduate students.
The survey demonstrates that students who take regular short breaks achieve better academic performance.

key_defence.learner_evidence: The visible evidence establishes self-reported good concentration in 72% of the regular-break group and 58% of the no-regular-break group, a difference of 14 percentage points. The study was observational, without random assignment or control of potentially relevant factors. Concentration was self-reported and academic performance was not measured.

alternatives.reason: It incorrectly converts an observed between-group association into a causal improvement.
It predicts an effect of introducing breaks and incorrectly describes the observed 14-percentage-point difference as 14%.
The survey concerned self-reported concentration, not measured academic performance.

items.feedback_note: The best-supported conclusion is that students who reported taking regular short breaks were more likely to report good concentration, but the survey does not establish that breaks caused the difference. The observed proportions were 72% and 58%, a difference of 14 percentage points, not an established 14% improvement. Because students were not randomly assigned and other potentially relevant factors were not controlled, the association cannot be treated as a causal effect. The survey also measured reported concentration rather than academic performance. The distinction matters because an explanation can communicate a meaningful finding without claiming more than the evidence warrants.

formative_return.forward_orientation: Consider whether your original explanation distinguishes the observed association from a claim that breaks caused better concentration. Apply that distinction where relevant when writing your revised explanation.

elicitations.evidence_ask: Elicit the principal authentic performance: an independently constructed revised explanation for a non-specialist audience that applies the learner's prioritised improvements and accurately communicates the numerical findings, evidential boundaries and relevant uncertainty.
elicitations.stimulus: Research evidence for your revised explanation: Study breaks and concentration among undergraduate students is a fictional, illustrative observational survey of 200 undergraduate students. Students reported their own study habits and concentration. Of the 100 students who reported taking regular short breaks during independent study, 72 reported good concentration (72%). Of the 100 who did not report taking regular short breaks, 58 reported good concentration (58%). The difference between the groups was 14 percentage points. Students were not randomly assigned, and potentially relevant factors including sleep, motivation, workload and study environment were not controlled. The survey does not establish that taking breaks caused better concentration, that reported concentration reflects objectively measured concentration or academic performance, or that the findings apply to all undergraduate students. It does not establish statistical significance, a confidence interval, or an optimal frequency or duration of breaks.

prompt.title: Learning Element 7: Write your revised explanation
prompt.context: You have identified the improvements you consider most important. Now apply those judgements to the same communication task: explaining the study's principal finding to someone without specialist research knowledge.
prompt.task: Write a new version of your explanation in your own words. Use the research evidence and your improvement priorities to make the explanation more accurate, informative and accessible. Communicate the numerical findings precisely, distinguish what the survey observed from what it cannot establish, and include the context or qualifications you judge most relevant. Make substantive changes rather than simply correcting surface errors. There is no single required wording or model answer.
prompt.response_expectation: A complete, independently written revised explanation that a non-specialist reader can follow. The explanation should accurately represent the observed findings and avoid unsupported causal claims.
prompt.suggested_length: One short paragraph or two concise paragraphs.

response_workspace.intention: Unrestricted sustained writing space for the learner's complete independently revised explanation, retained as the principal assessment artefact.
response_workspace.guidance: Write the explanation itself, not a list of proposed edits. Use your own judgement about which evidence and qualifications are most important for your audience.

materials.body: Read your revised explanation as though you were encountering the study for the first time. Can a non-specialist reader identify the main finding and the evidence supporting it? Check that any numerical comparison is precise: 72% and 58% differ by 14 percentage points. Consider whether your wording makes clear that concentration was self-reported and that the observational survey does not establish causation. Have you included the limitations most relevant to your claims without obscuring the main finding? Finally, compare this version with your initial explanation. Look for meaningful improvements in accuracy, reasoning, context or accessibility, not simply differences in wording. There is no single required explanation, and these questions are for your own judgement rather than an automatic assessment of your writing.

formative_return.forward_orientation: Your revised explanation is the main evidence of how you have applied your developing judgement. Keep it alongside your initial version so you can identify and explain the changes that matter most.

elicitations.evidence_ask: Elicit a concise learner-authored rationale linking the most significant changes between the initial and revised explanations to earlier diagnoses, research evidence and evaluative judgements.

prompt.title: Explain your most important changes
prompt.context: Your revised explanation is the main evidence of your developing capability. A short account of your decisions will help you examine that development later.
prompt.task: Identify the most significant changes you made between your initial and revised explanations. Explain why you made them and how they improve the explanation for a non-specialist reader. Refer to your earlier priorities, the research evidence or your developing judgements about quality where relevant.
prompt.response_expectation: A brief explanation of the most important revisions and their reasons, rather than a record of every wording change.

response_workspace.intention: Concise learner-authored rationale for significant revisions, retained alongside the revised explanation for subsequent reflection.
response_workspace.guidance: Focus on changes that made a meaningful difference to accuracy, reasoning or communication.

materials.body: Compare your reasons with the actual changes between your two explanations. Have you identified changes that are visible in the revised version? Does each reason explain why the change improves accuracy, evidential support, appropriate uncertainty or communication for your audience? Your rationale does not need to describe every edit. Its value lies in making the decisions behind significant improvements clear.

formative_return.forward_orientation: Keep your initial explanation, revised explanation and reasons for significant changes together. In 'The feedback that changed the work', use them to examine how your judgements developed and which changes most improved your work.

pack_forward_orientation: You have reconsidered your original explanation, selected improvements and produced an independent revision of the same research finding. The revised explanation is the principal evidence of your developing capability; the interpretation check and your written reasons provide different, more limited insights. No automatic judgement has been made about the quality of your unrestricted writing. Retain both versions of your explanation and your reasons for significant changes for 'The feedback that changed the work'. Comparing these materials will help you reflect on how your developing evaluative judgement influenced what you changed, what you retained and how effectively you communicated the evidence.
